1.pericope_label: The burden of the desert of the sea... A grievous vision is declared unto me; the treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously, and the spoiler spoileth

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the title from the catch-word of the following line and offers three accounts of the sea, the Euphrates, the surging flood of a mingled population, and the ancient description of the whole Euphrates plain, intersected with marshes and lakes, as looking like a sea; on the second verse he sees three successive tableaux, the Chaldaean power breaking treaties and removing landmarks, the summons to Elam and Media, and the oppressed ceasing to sigh, and answers the argument that pairing Elam with Media proves a late date by observing that Sargon was warring on both at the time. Delitzsch denies that the heading can have been drawn from the prophecy at all, since the word for sea never means the south but always the west and no sea appears in the oracle, which makes the heading peculiar rather than late; against the critics who assign the whole to a prophet at the close of the captivity he sets the possibility that prophetic insight reaches over hundreds of years.

Gill denies that Babylon was desert land and proposes either the desert lying between it and the countries its destroyers came from, or the sense plain, which suited Chaldea; he also notes that the vision is called hard, harsh not to the prophet or the Jews but to the Chaldeans. Calvin makes retaliation the point: Babylon had gained its power by plundering other nations and so seemed beyond danger, but having been a terror to others it could not avoid becoming a prey, and when a stone is hard a hard hammer will be found to break it.

Clarke divides the chapter before expounding it, into the taking of Babylon at a festival, an application to the Jews, a word on Dumah and a word on Arabia, and praises the first section as singular for brevity, force and rapidity of movement. On the second verse he reports that ten manuscripts omit a letter in one word and eight in another, which justifies the Greek version that rendered the clause passively, the plunderer plundered and the destroyer destroyed. Wesley gives the title in two halves, the plain of Babylon and the sea earned by the plenty of its waters, and says the Medes and Persians used treachery as well as force.
Henry takes the same flat country full of lakes, watered by the many streams of the Euphrates, and notes that some think it called a desert because a populous city was in time to become one.

debates.question: Why is Babylon called the desert of the sea?

positions.view: Either because a desert lay between it and its destroyers, or because the word may be rendered plain, as Chaldea was.
Because the flat country was full of lakes like little seas and watered by the Euphrates; or because a populous city would become a desert.
Because the whole Euphrates plain, intersected with marshes and lakes, looked like a sea to ancient observers.
The phrase cannot be drawn from the prophecy at all, since the word never means south and no sea appears in it; the heading is peculiar, not late.

debates.question: Is the treacherous dealer acting or suffering?

positions.view: Suffering: manuscript variation in a single letter justifies the passive rendering, the plunderer plundered and the destroyer destroyed.
Acting: the Chaldaean power is spoiling and breaking treaties until Elam and Media are summoned against it.

outliers.note: Turns the verse into an excursus on the authorship of the whole oracle, weighing the critics who date it to the end of the captivity against the possibility that prophetic insight reaches over centuries.
Reads the chapter first as a composition, praising its brevity, rapidity and energy of colouring, before treating it as prediction.

themes: The burden of the desert of the sea. As whirlwinds in the south pass through; so it cometh from the desert, from a terrible land.
A grievous vision is declared unto me; the treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously, and the spoiler spoileth. Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease.

3.pericope_label: Therefore are my loins filled with pain... And he saw a chariot with a couple of horsemen, a chariot of asses, and a chariot of camels

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the pangs for the prophet's own, the vision being so terrible that it overpowers all exultation and oppresses him like a nightmare, and calls the suggestion that he identifies himself with the Babylonians and their night of revelry hardly tenable; he reads the banquet verbs as indicative rather than imperative and reports rival renderings of the last clause as spreading the coverlet or taking a horoscope; and he renders the vision of the seventh verse a troop, a couple, grounding the animals in the record of asses and camels serving in the Persian army and appearing by the thousand in Assyrian spoil lists. Delitzsch reads the agitation as the prophet's own, supplies the unspoken link behind the connecting word, that they act so in Babylon because its destruction is determined, notes that elsewhere the prophet mans the watch-tower himself while here a distinct figure is posted, and rules out both riding-animals and war-chariots in favour of a troop seated upon animals advancing quietly in serried ranks.

Gill denies the pangs can be the prophet's, since Babylon was his people's mortal enemy and the ceasing of their sighing could be no distress to him but a joy, and puts the words in the mouth of the Babylonians and of Belshazzar; he keeps the banquet verbs as commands spoken to remove the king's fears, and names Cyrus and Darius as the riders. Calvin agrees that the prophet assumes for the time the character of a Babylonian in order to set the event before the eyes of the godly as in a mirror, allows the verbs may be participles, argues from the vividness that it was heavenly inspiration and not natural sagacity, since the ancient historian does not describe the storming so historically, and explains the doubled report by distance, the first glance being confused and only a nearer view making the objects plain.

Clarke takes the banquet verbs for infinitives absolute and renders them as statement, the table is prepared, on the analogy of a Latin idiom; he reports that several rabbins understood the verse of Belshazzar's feast and death, and that since a king is his people's defence he is himself the shield, so that anointing it means anointing a new king. He calls the seventh verse extremely obscure from the ambiguity of one word used three times, and suggests a cavalry in two parts or a force led by two riders, with the Medes and Persians distinguished by them. Wesley keeps the night of pleasure for the prophet's own repose while allowing that it signified the horror to fall on Babylon in a night of feasting, explains that shields were oiled to preserve and polish them, and reads the procession as abundant warlike provision.

debates.question: Whose are the pangs of the third verse?

positions.view: The Babylonians', and Belshazzar's in particular; they cannot be the prophet's, since Babylon's fall was his people's relief.
The Babylonians', by a deliberate device: the prophet assumes their character to set the event before the eyes of the godly.
The prophet's own; the identification with the Babylonians and their night of revelry is hardly tenable.
Both: the night of pleasure is the prophet's accustomed repose, and it also signified the horror to fall on Babylon at a feast.

debates.question: Are the verbs of the banquet verse commands or statements?

positions.view: Statements: they stand in the infinitive absolute and should be rendered the table is prepared.
Statements: better taken as indicative, they prepare and they watch.
Possibly participles: while they were preparing the table and setting a guard, sudden terror arose.
Commands, spoken by courtiers to remove the king's fears.

outliers.note: Reads the order to anoint the shield as an order to anoint a new king, the old one having just been killed at table.
Argues from the vividness of the description itself that the passage cannot be natural sagacity, since the ancient historian's account of the storming is less circumstantial than the prophet's.

themes: Therefore are my loins filled with pain: pangs have taken hold upon me, as the pangs of a woman that travaileth: I was bowed down at the hearing of it; I was dismayed at the seeing of it.
My heart panted, fearfulness affrighted me: the night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear unto me.
Prepare the table, watch in the watchtower, eat, drink: arise, ye princes, and anoint the shield.
For thus hath the Lord said unto me, Go, set a watchman, let him declare what he seeth.
And he saw a chariot with a couple of horsemen, a chariot of asses, and a chariot of camels; and he hearkened diligently with much heed:

8.pericope_label: And he cried, A lion: My lord, I stand continually upon the watchtower... O my threshing, and the corn of my floor

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the cry as a lion and hears the low murmur of an eager, almost angry impatience; he makes the announcement of the fall a second vision rather than the watchman's report of the first, notes that the stress falls on the smashing of the idols by iconoclastic Persians, identifies the child of the threshing-floor as Israel under invasion and exile, and adds that the prophet looks on those chastisements with yearning pity but cannot go beyond the word of the Lord, so that what lies between the present distress and the distant deliverance stays hidden. Delitzsch has the watchman growl like a lion, with the same dull angry sound and long breath out of full lungs, at having stood so long at his post for nothing; he sees at last that the procession had entered Babylon and mastered it, with a smaller troop returning to carry the news, and reads the threshing of Israel while warning against being misled by a later prophet who turned the same figure differently.

Gill has the watchman cry that he sees a lion, rejects the identification of that figure with named prophets, and makes it Cyrus at the head of the Median and Persian armies, a type of the Lion of Judah by whom mystical Babylon will fall; on the closing verse he allows the threshing might mean the Babylonians but prefers the Jews, whom the prophet calls his as his countrymen and whom God calls his floor and his corn. Calvin uses the standing watch to confirm the prophecy, since those God appoints to watch are neither drowsy nor dim-sighted; he denies that the herald can be the Babylonian king's watchman and weighs God, the conqueror, and the guardian of the vision as candidates, preferring God on the ground that the conqueror had no thought of overthrowing idols while allowing that the words suit an interpreting angel best; and he ends by saying that the splendour of the monarchy made the prediction of its ruin seem fabulous, so the prophet leads their minds to God.

Clarke calls the received reading of the lion so unintelligible that he does not doubt the true word is the seer, differing by a letter, and reports that the Syriac translator found it so and rendered it watchman; on the closing verse he glosses the address as spoken to whatever lies under the afflicting hand like corn spread on the floor to be threshed and winnowed, and notes that the translators used the word in a passive sense for the thing threshed. Wesley takes the lion for Cyrus or Darius leading their armies, assigns the explanation of the vision to the prophet and the act to God by Cyrus's hand, and alone thinks the threshing spoken of Babylon, explaining that the threshing stands for the corn threshed and the corn for a people sorely afflicted.

debates.question: What is the lion of the eighth verse?

positions.view: A person seen in the vision, namely Cyrus or Darius at the head of the armies.
A manner of crying out: the watchman's impatient, almost angry murmur, like a lion's growl.
Not in the text at all: the word is a corruption of the word for seer, as the Syriac version shows.

debates.question: Who is the threshing and the corn of the floor?

positions.view: Israel, under Assyrian and Chaldaean chastisement, with the wheat severed from the chaff.
Possibly the Babylonians, but more probably the Jews, God's own floor and corn, afflicted for their purging.
Probably Babylon; the threshing stands for the corn threshed and the corn for a people sorely afflicted.

outliers.note: Emends the text rather than explaining it, replacing the lion with the seer on the authority of the Syriac and the obviousness of the mistake.
Weighs three candidates for the herald of Babylon's fall and settles on an interpreting angel, on the ground that the human conqueror had no thought of overthrowing idols.

themes: And he cried, A lion: My lord, I stand continually upon the watchtower in the daytime, and I am set in my ward whole nights:
And, behold, here cometh a chariot of men, with a couple of horsemen. And he answered and said, Babylon is fallen, is fallen; and all the graven images of her gods he hath broken unto the ground.
O my threshing, and the corn of my floor: that which I have heard of the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared unto you.

11.pericope_label: The burden of Dumah. He calleth to me out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night?... The morning cometh, and also the night: if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come

schools.summary: Delitzsch reasons from the geography that a question called out of the mountains south of Palestine cannot be answered by any of the three known places bearing this name, in eastern Hauran, on the northern caravan road, or in the hills of Judah; on the reply he notes that it is deliberately cast in an Aramaic form of Hebrew and thinks Luther hit the sense, that when the morning comes it will still be night, though the connective cannot be stretched to mean and yet. Ellicott concludes that the name is mystical, Edom altered to a word meaning silence, so that as in the opening oracle the silence is first of expectancy and then of desolation; he reads the answer historically as a morning of hope whose day closes too quickly in blackness, summing up a future of one conqueror after another and the present desolation, and takes the prophet to decline further answer, so that the enquirers return from a bootless journey, rejecting the reading of that word as a call to repentance.

Gill reports that some rabbis take Dumah for the son of Ishmael and his Arabian descendants but holds for Edom, since Seir is named here and a separate word on Arabia follows, and notes that the Greek renders the title the vision of Idumea and that one rabbinic copy was found reading Edom outright; he hears in the answer a standing succession of morning and night, the gospel morning dispersing the shadows of the law, a night of blindness on the Jews, a morning at the Reformation, and a night now begun in coldness and error. Calvin alone keeps the descent from Ishmael and calls the people Dumeans; he makes the answer duration rather than sequence, the watchman saying in effect that what he tells them today he will tell them tomorrow, that wretched condition of hanging in doubt between death and life which was threatened as a curse through Moses, and offers two senses of the closing summons, that they lose their pains by running to and fro, or that the more anxious may go to Dumah and tremble worse there than at home.

Clarke reports the same variant reading Edom, gives the sense that the Jews would be delivered from captivity and the Edomites not, and then breaks off: what the last line means he cannot pretend to divine, and the Hebrew manuscripts give no assistance. Wesley takes the whole as a dialogue, the people of Dumah speaking by one of their number to a watchman set as men do in great danger and coming early to learn what the night had brought, the doubled question showing their solicitude; he makes the answer immediate, the night past without mischief and the light approaching but the morning soon gone and the night returning with their fears, and reads the closing summons as an appointment to come again next morning, and so from morning to morning.

Henry does not decide the identification but draws the use: some of Israel's neighbours are meant, and their distress foretold not only to prepare them but to warn Israel not to lean on any nation round about, for we must see creature confidences failing us, and feel them breaking under us, that we may not lay more weight on them than they will bear. The explication is difficult, he grants, because no history records the accomplishment, but the application is easy; and the one calling out of Seir was more concerned for the public safety than his countrymen, who were careless and secure.

positions.view: Edom, since Seir is named and a separate oracle on Arabia follows; ancient versions and one rabbinic copy read Edom outright.
Not any of the three known places of the name, none of which lies toward Seir.
A mystical name, Edom altered into the word for silence, matching the silence of expectancy and desolation.
The Arabian people descended from Ishmael's son of that name.

debates.question: What does the watchman mean by the morning coming and also the night?

positions.view: A standing succession of gospel mornings and nights running down to the present.
Edom's whole future: a morning of hope whose day closes quickly in blackness.
That the morning now approaching will pass and the night return with their fears.
That the anxiety will last, the same answer serving tomorrow as today.
That when the morning comes it will still be night, as Luther rendered it.

outliers.note: Declines to interpret the closing line at all, saying he cannot pretend to divine its meaning and that the manuscripts give no help.

themes: The burden of Dumah. He calleth to me out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?
The watchman said, The morning cometh, and also the night: if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come.

13.pericope_label: The burden upon Arabia. In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim... And the residue of the number of archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, shall be diminished

schools.summary: Delitzsch puts the difficulty of the heading in terms of the group: the other three take a simple genitive, and this one alone would be unsymbolic, so the added letter must have been introduced to make it symbolic, the prophet pointing it one way while holding the other in mind. Ellicott takes the alteration for a deliberate play, Arabia turned into a word for evening, the land spoken of being a land of shadow; he explains the oracle's point as the forcing of the Dedanite traders off their routes by Assyrian armies, has the men of Tema carry food out secretly for fear of the invader in strange contrast with Arab custom, observes that the fourfold repetition of the fuller preposition marks the stages of the retreat, says the formula of the hireling's years expresses the most precise measurement and so offers a test of the forecast, and hears in the word for residue the prophet's characteristic remnant, referring it to the Assyrian kings who record their victories over the Arabian tribes.

Gill keeps the Temanites as Arabians assisting their countrymen, and notes that the Kedarenes were expert with the bow for wild beasts and men alike, following their ancestor Ishmael. Calvin observes that the prophet leaves unnoticed none of the nations known to the Jews; he reads the bread and water as exhortation to meet a destitute people, reporting that some take the words instead as mockery of those who had been cruel to the Jews; he has the enemy pursue with arms so that flight is the only safety, the whole foretold so the Jews might learn that providence governs the world; he finds comfort in the nearness of the judgment, since we are naturally fiery and do not willingly bear delay; and he reads the diminishing of the remnant as pursuit of the ungodly to the utmost, where the punishment of the godly is moderated so they are not destroyed.

Clarke calls the title of doubtful authority, since it is missing from many Greek copies, since the word for burden is elsewhere joined to its object without a preposition, and since the same phrase stands as the second word of the prophecy itself, so that a marginal note might easily have slipped into the text; he reads the southern country for Tema with the Greek and Latin, on the ground that its men were probably caught in the same calamity and in no condition to help, adds that bringing out bread and water is ordinary humanity, the more so in deserts, transposes two words with the Latin to read the mighty bowmen, and compares the closing formula with the Roman verses on Cannae. Wesley reads the lodging in the forest as implying that a populous country would become wilderness, notes that travellers there went and still go in companies, makes the Dedanites merchants trading with Tyre, and takes the year for an exact year executed by the Assyrians.

Henry supplies the descent and the use: the Dedanites came from Abraham by Keturah and the men of Tema and Kedar from Ishmael, the Arabians lived in tents and kept cattle, and the Jews probably depended on them as a wall against the more warlike eastern nations, so that hearing this burden was meant to alarm them.

debates.question: Is the heading of this oracle sound?

positions.view: Doubtful: absent from many Greek copies, unlike the usual construction, and easily explained as a marginal note drawn from the prophecy's own second word.
Sound but symbolic: the unusual letter was introduced on purpose, the prophet pointing the word one way while meaning the other.
Sound and a deliberate play: Arabia altered into the word for evening, a land of shadow.

debates.question: What is happening when Tema brings out bread and water?

positions.view: Frightened hospitality: the men of Tema help secretly, fearing the invader, against all Arab custom.
An exhortation to meet a destitute people, though some read it as mockery of a cruel nation.
Nothing of the sort: the text should read the southern country, since Tema was caught in the same calamity and could not help.
Arabians relieving their own countrymen in distress.

outliers.note: Compares the prophecy's closing formula with the Roman verses foretelling the battle of Cannae, which end by saying Jupiter has thus spoken.

themes: The burden upon Arabia. In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim.
The inhabitants of the land of Tema brought water to him that was thirsty, they prevented with their bread him that fled.
For they fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, and from the bent bow, and from the grievousness of war.
For thus hath the Lord said unto me, Within a year, according to the years of an hireling, and all the glory of Kedar shall fail:
And the residue of the number of archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, shall be diminished: for the Lord God of Israel hath spoken it.
